evidence.observation: Historical past case (recorded demo scenario, 2026-09-23; not about today): SFO low-ceiling ground delay, evening deadline in San Francisco

data.title: SFO low-ceiling ground delay, evening deadline in San Francisco
data.situation: Fog and low ceilings put a Ground Delay Program on SFO arrivals (average 34 min) while JFK had no FAA program. Traveller needed to reach San Francisco the same evening.
data.decision: Compared JFK-SFO with EWR-OAK and EWR-SFO. Oakland was outside the SFO delay program and still about 30 minutes from San Francisco by BART or car.
data.outcome: Flying into OAK kept a larger arrival buffer than SFO; SFO stayed the backup if the program ended early.
data.lesson: A destination-airport delay program often does not apply to a neighbouring airport in the same metro. Check the other metro airports before accepting the delay.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-07; not about today): Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports

data.title: Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports
data.situation: Smoke from wildfires in eastern Canada blanketed New York on 7-8 June 2023 and reduced visibility for pilots. Ground delays hit LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia; average LaGuardia ground delays were reported at about two hours. On 8 June the FAA paused some flights bound for LaGuardia, later downgrading the stop to a ground delay.
data.decision: Low visibility from smoke acts like fog: it slows arrivals for hours or days. Strategy: allow for long ground delays into the affected airports and, for short Northeast trips, consider rail, which smoke affects far less.
data.outcome: Disruption lasted several days while the smoke persisted; New York's air quality index exceeded 400.
data.lesson: Wildfire smoke reduces arrival rates like fog does and can last for days; rail is a strong alternative for short trips.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-24; not about today): New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark

data.title: New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark
data.situation: From about 24 June 2023 thunderstorms in the New York area blocked arrival and departure routes at LaGuardia, JFK and Newark, and the FAA used ground stops and ground delay programs. Newark was hit hardest, with over 300 cancellations there; at one point the US had close to 7,800 delays and over 2,200 cancellations in a day.
data.decision: Summer storms in the Northeast typically build in the afternoon and evening. Strategy: choose an early-morning departure, keep a later backup, and for short Northeast trips consider rail, which storms affect less.
data.outcome: Disruption eased and returned over several days as storms recurred; United's Newark operation was among the worst affected.
data.lesson: In summer storm season, morning flights are the safest choice in the New York area, and rail is a strong backup for short trips.

data.title: Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports
data.situation: Smoke from wildfires in eastern Canada blanketed New York on 7-8 June 2023 and reduced visibility for pilots. Ground delays hit LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia; average LaGuardia ground delays were reported at about two hours. On 8 June the FAA paused some flights bound for LaGuardia, later downgrading the stop to a ground delay.
data.decision: Low visibility from smoke acts like fog: it slows arrivals for hours or days. Strategy: allow for long ground delays into the affected airports and, for short Northeast trips, consider rail, which smoke affects far less.
data.outcome: Disruption lasted several days while the smoke persisted; New York's air quality index exceeded 400.
data.lesson: Wildfire smoke reduces arrival rates like fog does and can last for days; rail is a strong alternative for short trips.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2018-03-02; not about today): March 2018 nor'easters: repeated storms shut flights and Amtrak in the Northeast

data.title: March 2018 nor'easters: repeated storms shut flights and Amtrak in the Northeast
data.situation: A series of nor'easters hit the Northeast in March 2018. In the 1-3 March storm Amtrak suspended Northeast Corridor service and more than 3,000 flights were cancelled. On 7 March about 2,787 flights were cancelled at airports including New York, Newark, Boston and Philadelphia, and on 21 March Winter Storm Toby caused more than 4,400 cancellations.
data.decision: Nor'easters affect air and rail along the whole corridor at once. Strategy: change the travel day rather than switch mode, because Amtrak is often reduced at the same time.
data.outcome: More than 10,000 Northeast flights were cancelled across the month's storms; Amtrak ran modified schedules and restored full corridor service after each storm.
data.lesson: In a nor'easter, rail is not a reliable backup for flights; moving the trip date is the safest option.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-24; not about today): New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark

data.title: New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark
data.situation: From about 24 June 2023 thunderstorms in the New York area blocked arrival and departure routes at LaGuardia, JFK and Newark, and the FAA used ground stops and ground delay programs. Newark was hit hardest, with over 300 cancellations there; at one point the US had close to 7,800 delays and over 2,200 cancellations in a day.
data.decision: Summer storms in the Northeast typically build in the afternoon and evening. Strategy: choose an early-morning departure, keep a later backup, and for short Northeast trips consider rail, which storms affect less.
data.outcome: Disruption eased and returned over several days as storms recurred; United's Newark operation was among the worst affected.
data.lesson: In summer storm season, morning flights are the safest choice in the New York area, and rail is a strong backup for short trips.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2012-10-29; not about today): Superstorm Sandy closes New York airports and halts Amtrak's Northeast Corridor

data.title: Superstorm Sandy closes New York airports and halts Amtrak's Northeast Corridor
data.situation: Superstorm Sandy hit the New York area on 29 October 2012. The three major New York airports closed, and Amtrak shut down its entire Northeast Corridor on 29-30 October. JFK and Newark began reopening on the morning of 31 October with limited schedules; LaGuardia, which had water on its runways, reopened last.
data.decision: A major coastal storm can shut air AND rail at the same time. Strategy: move travel well before the storm, because rail is not an independent backup when both are in the storm's path.
data.outcome: Air and rail service came back gradually over several days; Amtrak first restored modified service on parts of the corridor, and full service took longer.
data.lesson: Big storms can close airports and the railway together; the only safe plan is to travel before the storm or postpone.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-07; not about today): Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports

data.title: Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports
data.situation: Smoke from wildfires in eastern Canada blanketed New York on 7-8 June 2023 and reduced visibility for pilots. Ground delays hit LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia; average LaGuardia ground delays were reported at about two hours. On 8 June the FAA paused some flights bound for LaGuardia, later downgrading the stop to a ground delay.
data.decision: Low visibility from smoke acts like fog: it slows arrivals for hours or days. Strategy: allow for long ground delays into the affected airports and, for short Northeast trips, consider rail, which smoke affects far less.
data.outcome: Disruption lasted several days while the smoke persisted; New York's air quality index exceeded 400.
data.lesson: Wildfire smoke reduces arrival rates like fog does and can last for days; rail is a strong alternative for short trips.

data.situation: Fog and low ceilings put a Ground Delay Program on SFO arrivals (average 34 min) while JFK had no FAA program. Traveller needed to reach San Francisco the same evening.
data.decision: Compared JFK-SFO with EWR-OAK and EWR-SFO. Oakland was outside the SFO delay program and still about 30 minutes from San Francisco by BART or car.
data.outcome: Flying into OAK kept a larger arrival buffer than SFO; SFO stayed the backup if the program ended early.
data.lesson: A destination-airport delay program often does not apply to a neighbouring airport in the same metro. Check the other metro airports before accepting the delay.

data.title: Newark (EWR) radar and radio outage followed by weeks of delays
data.situation: On 28 April 2025 controllers at the Philadelphia facility that handles Newark traffic temporarily lost radar and radio contact with aircraft (reported as about 60-90 seconds). Several controllers then took trauma leave, worsening staffing. In early May the FAA ran a ground delay program for Newark arrivals with average delays reported at close to four hours, later reduced to about 2 hours 41 minutes.
data.decision: The problem was specific to one airport's air-traffic control and lasted for weeks. Strategy: use another airport in the same metro (JFK or LaGuardia) or, for Northeast Corridor trips, Amtrak.
data.outcome: Disruption at Newark continued for weeks and United issued travel waivers for Newark.
data.lesson: When one airport has a long-running equipment or staffing problem, a neighbouring airport in the same metro or the train is the most reliable backup.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-07; not about today): Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports

data.title: Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports
data.situation: Smoke from wildfires in eastern Canada blanketed New York on 7-8 June 2023 and reduced visibility for pilots. Ground delays hit LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia; average LaGuardia ground delays were reported at about two hours. On 8 June the FAA paused some flights bound for LaGuardia, later downgrading the stop to a ground delay.
data.decision: Low visibility from smoke acts like fog: it slows arrivals for hours or days. Strategy: allow for long ground delays into the affected airports and, for short Northeast trips, consider rail, which smoke affects far less.
data.outcome: Disruption lasted several days while the smoke persisted; New York's air quality index exceeded 400.
data.lesson: Wildfire smoke reduces arrival rates like fog does and can last for days; rail is a strong alternative for short trips.

data.situation: Fog and low ceilings put a Ground Delay Program on SFO arrivals (average 34 min) while JFK had no FAA program. Traveller needed to reach San Francisco the same evening.
data.decision: Compared JFK-SFO with EWR-OAK and EWR-SFO. Oakland was outside the SFO delay program and still about 30 minutes from San Francisco by BART or car.
data.outcome: Flying into OAK kept a larger arrival buffer than SFO; SFO stayed the backup if the program ended early.
data.lesson: A destination-airport delay program often does not apply to a neighbouring airport in the same metro. Check the other metro airports before accepting the delay.

data.title: New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark
data.situation: From about 24 June 2023 thunderstorms in the New York area blocked arrival and departure routes at LaGuardia, JFK and Newark, and the FAA used ground stops and ground delay programs. Newark was hit hardest, with over 300 cancellations there; at one point the US had close to 7,800 delays and over 2,200 cancellations in a day.
data.decision: Summer storms in the Northeast typically build in the afternoon and evening. Strategy: choose an early-morning departure, keep a later backup, and for short Northeast trips consider rail, which storms affect less.
data.outcome: Disruption eased and returned over several days as storms recurred; United's Newark operation was among the worst affected.
data.lesson: In summer storm season, morning flights are the safest choice in the New York area, and rail is a strong backup for short trips.

data.situation: Fog and low ceilings put a Ground Delay Program on SFO arrivals (average 34 min) while JFK had no FAA program. Traveller needed to reach San Francisco the same evening.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-07; not about today): Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports

data.title: Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports
data.situation: Smoke from wildfires in eastern Canada blanketed New York on 7-8 June 2023 and reduced visibility for pilots. Ground delays hit LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia; average LaGuardia ground delays were reported at about two hours. On 8 June the FAA paused some flights bound for LaGuardia, later downgrading the stop to a ground delay.
data.decision: Low visibility from smoke acts like fog: it slows arrivals for hours or days. Strategy: allow for long ground delays into the affected airports and, for short Northeast trips, consider rail, which smoke affects far less.
data.outcome: Disruption lasted several days while the smoke persisted; New York's air quality index exceeded 400.
data.lesson: Wildfire smoke reduces arrival rates like fog does and can last for days; rail is a strong alternative for short trips.

data.title: New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark
data.situation: From about 24 June 2023 thunderstorms in the New York area blocked arrival and departure routes at LaGuardia, JFK and Newark, and the FAA used ground stops and ground delay programs. Newark was hit hardest, with over 300 cancellations there; at one point the US had close to 7,800 delays and over 2,200 cancellations in a day.
data.decision: Summer storms in the Northeast typically build in the afternoon and evening. Strategy: choose an early-morning departure, keep a later backup, and for short Northeast trips consider rail, which storms affect less.
data.outcome: Disruption eased and returned over several days as storms recurred; United's Newark operation was among the worst affected.
data.lesson: In summer storm season, morning flights are the safest choice in the New York area, and rail is a strong backup for short trips.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-07; not about today): Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports

data.title: Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports
data.situation: Smoke from wildfires in eastern Canada blanketed New York on 7-8 June 2023 and reduced visibility for pilots. Ground delays hit LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia; average LaGuardia ground delays were reported at about two hours. On 8 June the FAA paused some flights bound for LaGuardia, later downgrading the stop to a ground delay.
data.decision: Low visibility from smoke acts like fog: it slows arrivals for hours or days. Strategy: allow for long ground delays into the affected airports and, for short Northeast trips, consider rail, which smoke affects far less.
data.outcome: Disruption lasted several days while the smoke persisted; New York's air quality index exceeded 400.
data.lesson: Wildfire smoke reduces arrival rates like fog does and can last for days; rail is a strong alternative for short trips.

data.title: Record rain floods Fort Lauderdale airport, closing it for about 40 hours
data.situation: Torrential rain (over 25 inches in South Florida within days) flooded Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International, which closed late on Wednesday 12 April 2023 for about 40 hours.
data.decision: A local flood closes one airport while nearby airports may still operate. Strategy: check other airports within driving distance (for Fort Lauderdale, Miami or Palm Beach) and expect reduced capacity after reopening.
data.outcome: The airport reopened at 9 a.m. on Friday 14 April with only one runway available, and cancellations and delays continued after reopening.
data.lesson: After a flood closure an airport often reopens with limited runways, so delays continue; a nearby airport can be the faster way out.

data.decision: Compared JFK-SFO with EWR-OAK and EWR-SFO. Oakland was outside the SFO delay program and still about 30 minutes from San Francisco by BART or car.

data.lesson: A destination-airport delay program often does not apply to a neighbouring airport in the same metro. Check the other metro airports before accepting the delay.

data.title: SFO low-ceiling ground delay, evening deadline in San Francisco
data.situation: Fog and low ceilings put a Ground Delay Program on SFO arrivals (average 34 min) while JFK had no FAA program. Traveller needed to reach San Francisco the same evening.
data.decision: Compared JFK-SFO with EWR-OAK and EWR-SFO. Oakland was outside the SFO delay program and still about 30 minutes from San Francisco by BART or car.
data.outcome: Flying into OAK kept a larger arrival buffer than SFO; SFO stayed the backup if the program ended early.
data.lesson: A destination-airport delay program often does not apply to a neighbouring airport in the same metro. Check the other metro airports before accepting the delay.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-24; not about today): New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark

data.title: New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark
data.situation: From about 24 June 2023 thunderstorms in the New York area blocked arrival and departure routes at LaGuardia, JFK and Newark, and the FAA used ground stops and ground delay programs. Newark was hit hardest, with over 300 cancellations there; at one point the US had close to 7,800 delays and over 2,200 cancellations in a day.
data.decision: Summer storms in the Northeast typically build in the afternoon and evening. Strategy: choose an early-morning departure, keep a later backup, and for short Northeast trips consider rail, which storms affect less.
data.outcome: Disruption eased and returned over several days as storms recurred; United's Newark operation was among the worst affected.
data.lesson: In summer storm season, morning flights are the safest choice in the New York area, and rail is a strong backup for short trips.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2025-04-28; not about today): Newark (EWR) radar and radio outage followed by weeks of delays

data.title: Newark (EWR) radar and radio outage followed by weeks of delays
data.situation: On 28 April 2025 controllers at the Philadelphia facility that handles Newark traffic temporarily lost radar and radio contact with aircraft (reported as about 60-90 seconds). Several controllers then took trauma leave, worsening staffing. In early May the FAA ran a ground delay program for Newark arrivals with average delays reported at close to four hours, later reduced to about 2 hours 41 minutes.
data.decision: The problem was specific to one airport's air-traffic control and lasted for weeks. Strategy: use another airport in the same metro (JFK or LaGuardia) or, for Northeast Corridor trips, Amtrak.
data.outcome: Disruption at Newark continued for weeks and United issued travel waivers for Newark.
data.lesson: When one airport has a long-running equipment or staffing problem, a neighbouring airport in the same metro or the train is the most reliable backup.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-07; not about today): Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports

data.title: Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports
data.situation: Smoke from wildfires in eastern Canada blanketed New York on 7-8 June 2023 and reduced visibility for pilots. Ground delays hit LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia; average LaGuardia ground delays were reported at about two hours. On 8 June the FAA paused some flights bound for LaGuardia, later downgrading the stop to a ground delay.
data.decision: Low visibility from smoke acts like fog: it slows arrivals for hours or days. Strategy: allow for long ground delays into the affected airports and, for short Northeast trips, consider rail, which smoke affects far less.
data.outcome: Disruption lasted several days while the smoke persisted; New York's air quality index exceeded 400.
data.lesson: Wildfire smoke reduces arrival rates like fog does and can last for days; rail is a strong alternative for short trips.

data.title: SFO low-ceiling ground delay, evening deadline in San Francisco
data.situation: Fog and low ceilings put a Ground Delay Program on SFO arrivals (average 34 min) while JFK had no FAA program. Traveller needed to reach San Francisco the same evening.
data.decision: Compared JFK-SFO with EWR-OAK and EWR-SFO. Oakland was outside the SFO delay program and still about 30 minutes from San Francisco by BART or car.
data.outcome: Flying into OAK kept a larger arrival buffer than SFO; SFO stayed the backup if the program ended early.
data.lesson: A destination-airport delay program often does not apply to a neighbouring airport in the same metro. Check the other metro airports before accepting the delay.

data.title: New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark
data.situation: From about 24 June 2023 thunderstorms in the New York area blocked arrival and departure routes at LaGuardia, JFK and Newark, and the FAA used ground stops and ground delay programs. Newark was hit hardest, with over 300 cancellations there; at one point the US had close to 7,800 delays and over 2,200 cancellations in a day.
data.decision: Summer storms in the Northeast typically build in the afternoon and evening. Strategy: choose an early-morning departure, keep a later backup, and for short Northeast trips consider rail, which storms affect less.
data.outcome: Disruption eased and returned over several days as storms recurred; United's Newark operation was among the worst affected.
data.lesson: In summer storm season, morning flights are the safest choice in the New York area, and rail is a strong backup for short trips.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-24; not about today): New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark

data.title: New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark
data.situation: From about 24 June 2023 thunderstorms in the New York area blocked arrival and departure routes at LaGuardia, JFK and Newark, and the FAA used ground stops and ground delay programs. Newark was hit hardest, with over 300 cancellations there; at one point the US had close to 7,800 delays and over 2,200 cancellations in a day.
data.decision: Summer storms in the Northeast typically build in the afternoon and evening. Strategy: choose an early-morning departure, keep a later backup, and for short Northeast trips consider rail, which storms affect less.
data.outcome: Disruption eased and returned over several days as storms recurred; United's Newark operation was among the worst affected.
data.lesson: In summer storm season, morning flights are the safest choice in the New York area, and rail is a strong backup for short trips.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-04-12; not about today): Record rain floods Fort Lauderdale airport, closing it for about 40 hours

data.title: Record rain floods Fort Lauderdale airport, closing it for about 40 hours
data.situation: Torrential rain (over 25 inches in South Florida within days) flooded Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International, which closed late on Wednesday 12 April 2023 for about 40 hours.
data.decision: A local flood closes one airport while nearby airports may still operate. Strategy: check other airports within driving distance (for Fort Lauderdale, Miami or Palm Beach) and expect reduced capacity after reopening.
data.outcome: The airport reopened at 9 a.m. on Friday 14 April with only one runway available, and cancellations and delays continued after reopening.
data.lesson: After a flood closure an airport often reopens with limited runways, so delays continue; a nearby airport can be the faster way out.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2025-06-27; not about today): Atlanta hail and thunderstorms: ground stop, diversions and days of Delta cancellations

data.title: Atlanta hail and thunderstorms: ground stop, diversions and days of Delta cancellations
data.situation: On the evening of 27 June 2025 storms with hail and strong winds hit Atlanta and a ground stop was issued. Delta reported more than 90 diversions and pulled over 50 aircraft for safety checks; on Saturday 28 June it had 542 cancellations across its network.
data.decision: Atlanta is Delta's main hub, so a storm there spreads across the airline's network for days. Strategy: avoid connecting through the affected hub the next day too, and prefer a non-stop or another hub.
data.outcome: Cancellations continued the following day while aircraft were inspected and crews repositioned.
data.lesson: A severe storm at a hub causes knock-on cancellations the next day. Avoid connecting through that hub until it has clearly recovered.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (recorded demo scenario, 2026-09-23; not about today): SFO low-ceiling ground delay, evening deadline in San Francisco

data.title: SFO low-ceiling ground delay, evening deadline in San Francisco
data.situation: Fog and low ceilings put a Ground Delay Program on SFO arrivals (average 34 min) while JFK had no FAA program. Traveller needed to reach San Francisco the same evening.
data.decision: Compared JFK-SFO with EWR-OAK and EWR-SFO. Oakland was outside the SFO delay program and still about 30 minutes from San Francisco by BART or car.
data.outcome: Flying into OAK kept a larger arrival buffer than SFO; SFO stayed the backup if the program ended early.
data.lesson: A destination-airport delay program often does not apply to a neighbouring airport in the same metro. Check the other metro airports before accepting the delay.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-07; not about today): Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports

data.title: Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports
data.situation: Smoke from wildfires in eastern Canada blanketed New York on 7-8 June 2023 and reduced visibility for pilots. Ground delays hit LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia; average LaGuardia ground delays were reported at about two hours. On 8 June the FAA paused some flights bound for LaGuardia, later downgrading the stop to a ground delay.
data.decision: Low visibility from smoke acts like fog: it slows arrivals for hours or days. Strategy: allow for long ground delays into the affected airports and, for short Northeast trips, consider rail, which smoke affects far less.
data.outcome: Disruption lasted several days while the smoke persisted; New York's air quality index exceeded 400.
data.lesson: Wildfire smoke reduces arrival rates like fog does and can last for days; rail is a strong alternative for short trips.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2018-03-02; not about today): March 2018 nor'easters: repeated storms shut flights and Amtrak in the Northeast

data.title: March 2018 nor'easters: repeated storms shut flights and Amtrak in the Northeast
data.situation: A series of nor'easters hit the Northeast in March 2018. In the 1-3 March storm Amtrak suspended Northeast Corridor service and more than 3,000 flights were cancelled. On 7 March about 2,787 flights were cancelled at airports including New York, Newark, Boston and Philadelphia, and on 21 March Winter Storm Toby caused more than 4,400 cancellations.
data.decision: Nor'easters affect air and rail along the whole corridor at once. Strategy: change the travel day rather than switch mode, because Amtrak is often reduced at the same time.
data.outcome: More than 10,000 Northeast flights were cancelled across the month's storms; Amtrak ran modified schedules and restored full corridor service after each storm.
data.lesson: In a nor'easter, rail is not a reliable backup for flights; moving the trip date is the safest option.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-07; not about today): Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports

data.title: Canadian wildfire smoke cuts visibility at New York airports
data.situation: Smoke from wildfires in eastern Canada blanketed New York on 7-8 June 2023 and reduced visibility for pilots. Ground delays hit LaGuardia, Newark and Philadelphia; average LaGuardia ground delays were reported at about two hours. On 8 June the FAA paused some flights bound for LaGuardia, later downgrading the stop to a ground delay.
data.decision: Low visibility from smoke acts like fog: it slows arrivals for hours or days. Strategy: allow for long ground delays into the affected airports and, for short Northeast trips, consider rail, which smoke affects far less.
data.outcome: Disruption lasted several days while the smoke persisted; New York's air quality index exceeded 400.
data.lesson: Wildfire smoke reduces arrival rates like fog does and can last for days; rail is a strong alternative for short trips.

evidence.observation: Historical past case (recorded demo scenario, 2026-09-23; not about today): SFO low-ceiling ground delay, evening deadline in San Francisco

data.title: SFO low-ceiling ground delay, evening deadline in San Francisco
data.situation: Fog and low ceilings put a Ground Delay Program on SFO arrivals (average 34 min) while JFK had no FAA program. Traveller needed to reach San Francisco the same evening.
data.decision: Compared JFK-SFO with EWR-OAK and EWR-SFO. Oakland was outside the SFO delay program and still about 30 minutes from San Francisco by BART or car.
data.outcome: Flying into OAK kept a larger arrival buffer than SFO; SFO stayed the backup if the program ended early.
data.lesson: A destination-airport delay program often does not apply to a neighbouring airport in the same metro. Check the other metro airports before accepting the delay.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2018-03-02; not about today): March 2018 nor'easters: repeated storms shut flights and Amtrak in the Northeast

data.title: March 2018 nor'easters: repeated storms shut flights and Amtrak in the Northeast
data.situation: A series of nor'easters hit the Northeast in March 2018. In the 1-3 March storm Amtrak suspended Northeast Corridor service and more than 3,000 flights were cancelled. On 7 March about 2,787 flights were cancelled at airports including New York, Newark, Boston and Philadelphia, and on 21 March Winter Storm Toby caused more than 4,400 cancellations.
data.decision: Nor'easters affect air and rail along the whole corridor at once. Strategy: change the travel day rather than switch mode, because Amtrak is often reduced at the same time.
data.outcome: More than 10,000 Northeast flights were cancelled across the month's storms; Amtrak ran modified schedules and restored full corridor service after each storm.
data.lesson: In a nor'easter, rail is not a reliable backup for flights; moving the trip date is the safest option.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2023-06-24; not about today): New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark

data.title: New York summer thunderstorms block routes at JFK, LaGuardia and Newark
data.situation: From about 24 June 2023 thunderstorms in the New York area blocked arrival and departure routes at LaGuardia, JFK and Newark, and the FAA used ground stops and ground delay programs. Newark was hit hardest, with over 300 cancellations there; at one point the US had close to 7,800 delays and over 2,200 cancellations in a day.
data.decision: Summer storms in the Northeast typically build in the afternoon and evening. Strategy: choose an early-morning departure, keep a later backup, and for short Northeast trips consider rail, which storms affect less.
data.outcome: Disruption eased and returned over several days as storms recurred; United's Newark operation was among the worst affected.
data.lesson: In summer storm season, morning flights are the safest choice in the New York area, and rail is a strong backup for short trips.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2012-10-29; not about today): Superstorm Sandy closes New York airports and halts Amtrak's Northeast Corridor

data.title: Superstorm Sandy closes New York airports and halts Amtrak's Northeast Corridor
data.situation: Superstorm Sandy hit the New York area on 29 October 2012. The three major New York airports closed, and Amtrak shut down its entire Northeast Corridor on 29-30 October. JFK and Newark began reopening on the morning of 31 October with limited schedules; LaGuardia, which had water on its runways, reopened last.
data.decision: A major coastal storm can shut air AND rail at the same time. Strategy: move travel well before the storm, because rail is not an independent backup when both are in the storm's path.
data.outcome: Air and rail service came back gradually over several days; Amtrak first restored modified service on parts of the corridor, and full service took longer.
data.lesson: Big storms can close airports and the railway together; the only safe plan is to travel before the storm or postpone.

evidence.subject: past_case
evidence.observation: Historical past case (real event from public reports, 2018-03-02; not about today): March 2018 nor'easters: repeated storms shut flights and Amtrak in the Northeast

data.title: March 2018 nor'easters: repeated storms shut flights and Amtrak in the Northeast
data.situation: A series of nor'easters hit the Northeast in March 2018. In the 1-3 March storm Amtrak suspended Northeast Corridor service and more than 3,000 flights were cancelled. On 7 March about 2,787 flights were cancelled at airports including New York, Newark, Boston and Philadelphia, and on 21 March Winter Storm Toby caused more than 4,400 cancellations.
data.decision: Nor'easters affect air and rail along the whole corridor at once. Strategy: change the travel day rather than switch mode, because Amtrak is often reduced at the same time.
data.outcome: More than 10,000 Northeast flights were cancelled across the month's storms; Amtrak ran modified schedules and restored full corridor service after each storm.
data.lesson: In a nor'easter, rail is not a reliable backup for flights; moving the trip date is the safest option.
